possum.types: Textile possum fiber is the underfur of the brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula) from New Zealand, sold almost only in blends. The main trade forms are plucked fur, possum-merino knitting yarns and knitwear, and dressed possum pelts used for fur trims and throws, a separate product. Blends are defined by the possum share. Zealana, a New Zealand yarn brand, lists its Kauri worsted as 60 percent merino, 30 percent possum and 10 percent mulberry silk, and its Air range as 40 percent possum, 40 percent cashmere and 20 percent silk. Retail knitwear typically uses merino as the majority fiber with possum as a substantial minority, and silk or nylon added for strength and luster.
possum.fabrics: Most possum fiber ends up in knitted garments: jerseys, cardigans, beanies, scarves, gloves and socks, plus hand-knitting yarns from lace to worsted weight. Possum-merino socks and gloves are sold for outdoor and travel use. Silk-containing blends give drape and sheen for lighter shawls and fine-gauge knits. The possum share produces a soft halo on the knit surface. Fabrics are almost always knitted rather than woven, because the short, slippery fur needs the loft and give of a knit structure.
possum.quality: Read the percentage label: a higher possum share gives more halo and softness but can shed more early in wear, and very low percentages add little. Feel for a light, soft, fuzzy surface with no harsh fibers. Check that labels say possum or brushtail possum, not opossum, rabbit or generic fur fiber, since cheaper haloed yarns can imitate the look. Ask whether the yarn was made in New Zealand, as most possum processing happens there. Claims of extra warmth or pill resistance are producer statements; pilling can be tested by standard methods such as ISO 12945-2 if a buyer needs data.
pros: Possum adds a light, soft halo and loft to merino without much added weight.
Blends are commonly described by producers as warm for their weight.
The fiber comes from an introduced pest that New Zealand already controls to protect native forest.
Merino in the blend supplies elasticity and shape retention.
cons: Pure possum yarn is impractical, so the fiber is always blended and the possum share varies.
Short fibers can shed from the surface, especially in the first wears.
Supply depends on pest control and would shrink if eradication goals succeed.
Fiber comes from killed animals, which some buyers reject regardless of the pest context.
possum.impact: Possums are culled in New Zealand to protect native forest and birds and to control bovine tuberculosis, and fur recovery adds value to part of that control. An Envirolink report for regional councils estimated about 30 million possums after control efforts, lower than earlier estimates of 50 to 70 million. Whether commercial fur harvest aids conservation is contested: a 2012 study in Biological Conservation found that harvesting for economic return and controlling possums for biodiversity outcomes can pull in different directions, because hunters target accessible, high-yield areas rather than sites with the highest ecological priority. Animal welfare depends on trapping and poisoning methods. Processing impacts are mainly those of merino scouring and spinning.
possum.care: Hand wash in cool water with a gentle wool detergent unless the label states machine washable; some producers treat blends for machine washing on a wool cycle. Avoid hot water, agitation and wringing, which felt both the merino and the possum fibers. Rinse at the same temperature, roll in a towel and dry flat in shape. Do not tumble dry. Light shedding in the first few wears is normal; a lint roller or gentle brushing removes loose fibers. Press only with a cool iron through a damp cloth or use steam. Store folded, not hung, with a moth deterrent. The product label governs.
faq: Is possum fur the same as opossum?

No. Textile possum comes from the Australian brushtail possum, Trichosurus vulpecula, introduced to New Zealand in the nineteenth century. The American opossum, Didelphis, is a different marsupial whose fur is a separate, minor product.
Why is possum always blended with merino?
Brushtail possum underfur is short and slippery, so it does not hold together in a yarn by itself. Merino provides fiber length, crimp and cohesion, and silk or nylon may be added for strength.
Is buying possum merino good for the environment?

Possums damage New Zealand's native forests and are controlled for that reason. Using their fur adds value to control work, but research has found that commercial harvest and conservation goals do not always coincide, so treat blanket conservation claims cautiously.

Some shedding is common in the first wears as loose, short possum fibers work free from the yarn surface. It usually settles down after a few wears and gentle washing. Heavy, continuing shedding suggests a loosely spun yarn or a high possum share.
notable: An Envirolink report estimated New Zealand's possum population at about 30 million, down from earlier estimates of 50 to 70 million.
Commercial possum hunting has been called a mixed blessing for conservation because hunters seek fur where it is easy to take, not where native forest is most at risk.
Possum-merino yarns are among the few mainstream knitting yarns made from the fur of an animal officially classed as a pest.
